items.recapEn: At the river-crossing museum a volunteer guide, Nomura-san, explained how porters once carried travellers across the Ōi on their shoulders, with fares set by the water's depth. He asked why Hana and Ken walk; the answer took many 'um's and 'I see's. Ken took Tamura-san's tea-farm kitchen until autumn; Hana stayed to fill her diary. Kyoto? 'In winter, probably.'

items.recapEn: On the old stone slope Hana asked Ken if he was really staying. He was: it's a kitchen, isn't it, and Tamura-san's has big pots and a window onto the tea fields. Hana will stay too and fill the empty pages. Ken's pack had gained a jar of Kanaya tea, 'light'. At the top, the wide river shone.

items.recapEn: A museum notice: long ago the Ōi had no bridge or boats; porters carried travellers on their shoulders, the fare set each morning by the water's depth, and when it ran too deep everyone waited for days. Rules: touch nothing, photos welcome, bags at reception, mind the stone slope in rain, free guides, cold Kanaya tea at the exit.
